subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Sassoon's satirical war poems differ from Owen's elegiac mode chiefly through their:
options: Bitter irony and savage attack on those who prolonged the war from safety
Refusal to mention soldiers
Pastoral celebration of the home front
Tender pity and hushed tones
questions.explain: Sassoon often deploys biting irony to indict generals, politicians and complacent civilians.

questions.q: 'Texts in shared contexts' asks students to study works grouped by a common:
options: Publisher
Page count
Social, historical or political context such as WWI or the changing role of women
Author surname
questions.explain: The component clusters texts around a shared context, exploring how period and society shape literature.

questions.q: Studying literature 'in shared contexts' assumes that grouping texts by context helps reveal:
options: Nothing beyond the individual text
Patterns, dialogues and contrasts in how writers respond to the same conditions
Only the texts' publication dates
That all texts of a period are identical
questions.explain: Clustering by context illuminates how different writers engage, variously, with shared circumstances.

questions.q: A post-colonial reading of a canonical text might 'write back' by:
options: Exposing the text's imperial assumptions or giving voice to the colonised perspective it marginalised
Focusing only on metre
Removing all context
Praising the empire uncritically
questions.explain: 'Writing back' challenges imperial viewpoints and recovers the perspectives empire silenced.

questions.q: The idea that context shapes a text's 'reception' means that:
options: How readers interpret and value a text changes with their own historical and cultural situation
Texts mean exactly the same to every reader in every era
Context only affects the author, never readers
Reception is irrelevant to literary study
questions.explain: Reception theory recognises that meaning and value are shaped by the reader's own context, not fixed forever.

questions.q: The literature of the First World War (Owen, Sassoon) is often distinguished from earlier patriotic verse by its:
options: Use of pastoral idyll only
Avoidance of any reference to combat
Unflinching depiction of suffering, futility and disillusionment
Celebration of war's glory and heroism
questions.explain: Owen and Sassoon expose the horror and futility of trench warfare, countering older glorifying conventions.

questions.q: 'Protest' or political writing is characterised by its intention to:
options: Avoid all reference to society
Challenge injustice, power or oppression and provoke the reader to question the status quo
Entertain without any social purpose
Describe nature for its own sake
questions.explain: Protest literature is purposive, contesting injustice and inviting critique of prevailing power.

questions.q: In the context of 'modern times', T. S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land' is frequently read as expressing:
options: Optimistic faith in imperial expansion
The spiritual barrenness and fragmentation of post-war modern civilisation
A simple love story
A celebration of rural festivals
questions.explain: Eliot's fragmented, allusive poem is read as diagnosing the sterility and disorder of the modern world.

questions.q: The 'changing role of women' as a shared context allows study of how literature reflects and shapes shifts in:
options: Women's social, legal and economic status across periods
Military tactics only
Astronomical discovery
The chemistry of dyes
questions.explain: Texts can be read against evolving expectations, rights and roles of women over time.

questions.q: Modernism as a literary context responds to 'modern times' by registering:
options: A return to medieval romance
A sense of fragmentation, alienation and the breakdown of old certainties after industrialisation and war
Indifference to changing society
Confidence in steady moral and social progress
questions.explain: Modernist writing reflects a fractured, disorientating modernity, often through fragmented form and alienated voices.

questions.q: Wilfred Owen's stated aim that 'the Poetry is in the pity' signals that his war poetry seeks to:
options: Glorify the nation's military triumph
Celebrate technological progress
Convey compassion for the suffering of soldiers and protest war's waste
Provide neutral battlefield reportage
questions.explain: Owen foregrounds pity and protest, exposing the human cost of war rather than glorifying it.

questions.q: When applying context, the strongest essays treat historical material as:
options: A lens that illuminates specific choices of language, form and meaning in the text
A substitute for reading the text
A fixed set of facts to be recited at the start
Decoration with no analytical purpose
questions.explain: Context works best as an interpretive lens tied to particular textual details, not recitation.

questions.q: The danger of 'context as bolt-on' refers to:
options: Pasting in historical or biographical information that does not actually illuminate the text's meaning
Comparing two texts
Using context to deepen interpretation
Analysing the poem's form
questions.explain: Bolt-on context is irrelevant background dropped in without connecting to how the text creates meaning.

questions.q: A nuanced view of the relationship between literature and its period holds that texts:
options: Are wholly untouched by history
Both reflect their context and can question, resist or reshape it
Can only ever endorse the values of their time
Merely passively mirror their society
questions.explain: Literature does not just mirror its age; it can also critique, subvert or intervene in it.

questions.q: The contextual study of gender in literature considers how texts may:
options: Only ever reinforce traditional roles
Either reinforce or subvert the gender expectations of their period
Be written only by men
Never engage with gender
questions.explain: Texts can both uphold and challenge the gender norms of their time, and analysis should weigh which.

questions.q: The phrase 'literature does not exist in a vacuum' captures the principle that:
options: Texts are produced and read within social, historical and ideological conditions that bear on their meaning
Only science is shaped by context
Texts should be read without any reference to the world
Context applies only to non-fiction
questions.explain: This principle underpins AO3: texts are embedded in, and engage with, their world.

questions.q: Recognising that an interpretation is itself shaped by the critic's context means accepting that:
options: Context applies only to authors
Critical readings (e.g. Marxist, feminist, post-colonial) reflect particular values and questions
Criticism is unaffected by ideology
There is only one timeless 'correct' reading
questions.explain: Critical approaches are themselves historically and ideologically situated, generating different readings.

questions.q: AO3 (context) is best handled in an essay by:
options: Weaving relevant context into analysis to illuminate how it shapes the text's meaning and reception
Ignoring context entirely
Listing every event of the period
Adding a separate paragraph of historical facts unconnected to the text
questions.explain: Strong AO3 use integrates context with close analysis rather than treating it as a detachable 'bolt-on'.

questions.q: To say a text is shaped by its 'context of production' is to consider:
options: The historical, social and personal circumstances in which it was written
Its print font
The price of the first edition
Only how modern readers respond to it
questions.explain: Context of production concerns the conditions under which a work was created, distinct from its later reception.

questions.q: The most sophisticated use of AO3 demonstrates that context can affect:
options: Neither meaning nor interpretation
Only the length of the text
Both the meaning a text generated when produced and the varied meanings readers find across time
Only the author's intentions
questions.explain: Advanced contextual study links context to production and to shifting reception, enriching interpretation.

questions.q: The risk of 'over-contextualising' a text is that:
options: Historical detail crowds out close reading, so the text itself is neglected
The essay becomes too short
The analysis becomes too close to the words on the page
Context can never be excessive
questions.explain: Excessive context can swamp engagement with the actual language and effects of the text.

questions.q: Post-colonial writing typically engages with:
options: The legacies of colonialism, including identity, displacement, language and the contesting of imperial narratives
Medieval courtly love
The natural sciences only
The glorification of empire
questions.explain: Post-colonial literature interrogates the experience and aftermath of colonisation, reclaiming voice and history.

questions.q: In 'texts in shared contexts', comparing a text written during an event with one written long after it allows students to explore:
options: Nothing of analytical value
Which author was wealthier
How temporal distance and hindsight shape representation of the same context
Only differences in spelling
questions.explain: Contemporary and retrospective treatments of the same context reveal how perspective and hindsight alter representation.

questions.q: A Marxist-influenced contextual reading would foreground a text's engagement with:
options: Only the weather imagery
The author's eye colour
Rhyme and metre exclusively
Class, power, labour and economic relations within the society depicted
questions.explain: Marxist criticism attends to class conflict, power and the material/economic conditions a text reflects or critiques.

questions.q: 'Foregrounding' in stylistic analysis means:
options: describing the background setting
making a linguistic feature prominent through deviation or repetition so it draws attention
summarising the plot's opening
placing a scene at the front of the play
questions.explain: Foregrounding makes language conspicuous through patterning or deviation, directing the reader's interpretive attention.

questions.q: 'Dramatic irony' occurs when:
options: the play breaks the fourth wall
the audience knows something a character on stage does not
a character speaks in verse while others speak in prose
the chorus comments on the action
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises from the gap between the audience's knowledge and a character's ignorance of it.

questions.q: In narrative theory, 'free indirect discourse' is best defined as:
options: a character's thoughts rendered in the third person yet inflected with that character's own idiom and feeling
a first-person narrator addressing the reader directly
direct speech reported within quotation marks
an authorial commentary that judges the characters explicitly
questions.explain: Free indirect discourse blends the narrator's third-person report with a character's voice, blurring the line between the two.

questions.q: A 'Marxist' reading of a novel would be most likely to foreground:
options: the protagonist's Oedipal anxieties
the author's use of assonance
class, labour, ideology and the material conditions shaping the characters
the sublime grandeur of the landscape
questions.explain: Marxist criticism analyses class conflict, ideology and how material and economic forces shape texts and characters.

questions.q: A 'new historicist' reading of a literary text would most characteristically:
options: judge the text purely by its formal elegance and unity
focus only on the reader's emotional response
read the text as a timeless expression of universal human nature
treat the text as one of many cultural documents circulating within and shaping the power relations of its period
questions.explain: New historicism situates a text among the period's other discourses, reading literature and history as mutually constitutive.

questions.q: The most sophisticated use of a critical quotation is to:
options: engage with it dialectically, qualifying or contesting it through close textual evidence
ignore it entirely
agree with it uncritically
place it at the end as a flourish
questions.explain: AO5 rewards a critical dialogue with other readings, tested against the student's own analysis of the text.
